We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement. 1. Introduction New World orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a rapidly progressive illness characterized by capillary leak, pulmonary edema, shock, and, in severe cases, cardiorespiratory failure. The syndrome was recognized internationally after the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States, and subsequent surveillance established a heterogeneous distribution of pathogenic orthohantaviruses across North, Central, and South America. Although HCPS is uncommon compared with many endemic infections, case fatality remains substantial and varies by virus, setting, clinical recognition, and access to supportive care. The major New World viruses illustrate why a single continental model is inadequate. Sin Nombre virus (SNV) predominates among recognized cases in the United States, Andes virus (ANDV) is a major cause of HCPS in Argentina and Chile and can be transmitted from person to person, and Choclo virus (CHOV) sustains endemic transmission in Panama. South America also contains extensive viral and reservoir diversity, including Juquitiba- and Araraquara-associated transmission systems in Brazil. This diversity affects reservoir ecology, transmission opportunities, immune interactions, and the design of surveillance systems. Hantavirus risk is usually described through the climate–rodent–human interface. Climatic variability and landscape change influence vegetation and food availability, which can alter reservoir abundance and movement; housing, occupation, and human behavior then shape whether infected rodents and people share the same spaces. That ecological pathway is necessary but incomplete. Exposure does not invariably produce infection, and infection does not invariably progress to severe HCPS. The transition from infection to clinical disease depends on viral entry, innate sensing and immune evasion, endothelial barrier regulation, cellular immune responses, and humoral immunity. The final transition, from clinically apparent infection to a documented outcome, also depends on case ascertainment and care pathways. Early HCPS symptoms are nonspecific, confirmatory assays and referral services vary across settings, and severe disease may require specialized critical care. These conditions plausibly affect recognition and management, although available comparative studies do not quantify their independent contribution to differences in case fatality. Serosurveys from particular Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous geographic and exposure contexts; they do not support assumptions of ethnicity-based intrinsic biological susceptibility. This review examines how ecological exposure, host immune responses, and structural conditions may be connected along a mechanism-to-population continuum, with emphasis on settings for which primary human and reservoir evidence is available. Its purpose is to identify supported links and explicitly distinguish them from cross-level hypotheses that require prospective testing. 2. Methodology We conducted a critical narrative review integrating clinical, epidemiological, ecological, and mechanistic evidence on New World orthohantaviruses in the Americas within a One Health framework. The literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos, and LILACS, from database inception through 29 September 2026, without language restrictions. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH/DeCS), where applicable, and free-text terms adapted to each database, covering hantaviruses and relevant New World viruses, reservoir ecology, climate, land use, transmission, immunopathogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, clinical management, surveillance, and structural determinants of health (Supplementary Tables S1–S4). The PubMed/MEDLINE search was updated on 27 October 2026. Additional relevant publications were identified through reference-list screening. Institutional public-health reports and peer-reviewed surveillance studies were selected based on source credibility, geographic relevance, temporal coverage, and traceability to provide complementary context on regional epidemiological patterns, surveillance activities, and public-health responses. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts, and potentially relevant full texts, resolving disagreements through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Publications were selected based on relevance, directness of evidence, and contextual applicability. Priority was given to clinical and epidemiological investigations, reservoir and environmental studies, and experimental research with mechanistic relevance. Relevant reviews and reports from recognized national or regional public-health institutions were also considered. Publications with limited thematic relevance, insufficiently supported findings, or unclear geographic or ecological applicability were not prioritized. Seventy-six sources are cited in this review. Relevant information was extracted on study design, geographic setting, viral species, study population or ecological context, principal findings, and methodological limitations. Evidence was organized and synthesized thematically, considering consistency across studies, directness of findings, and inferential limitations. Experimental evidence, observational associations, and proposed mechanistic or population-level relationships were distinguished during interpretation. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or certainty-of-evidence grading was performed for individual studies. The Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) informed the scientific reasoning, referencing, and presentation of the review (Supplementary Table S8). Figures were prepared using BioRender, including its integrated generative artificial intelligence tools. 3. Viral Diversity and Reservoir Ecology Across the Americas Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with segmented genomes. In the Americas, clinically important lineages are maintained primarily in sigmodontine and neotomine rodents, although viral RNA or antibodies have been detected in additional small-mammal species. Detection in a species is not sufficient to establish reservoir competence; a competent reservoir must sustain infection and contribute to onward viral maintenance and shedding. In North America, SNV is the dominant recognized cause of HCPS in the United States and is strongly associated with the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. Surveillance identifies heterogeneity in location and genotype, but reports from the United States should not be extrapolated uncritically to Canada or Mexico. A 2019 review of Mexico found multiple rodent-associated hantaviruses but no confirmed human hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the publications assessed at that time. Canada, by contrast, has a documented national experience: 143 laboratory-confirmed SNV-associated HCPS cases had been reported up to 1 January 2020, together with a reviewed account of local ecology, biology, and viral genetics. Caribbean evidence is sparser but not absent; in Barbados, retrospective and prospective testing of patients with febrile illness detected orthohantavirus-specific antibodies between 2008 and 2016, with higher prevalence during the rainy season and among urban residents. For much of the remaining Caribbean and for large parts of Mexico, the evidence assembled here is too sparse for a comparable synthesis of human burden, virus diversity, or reservoir dynamics; an absence of studies should not be interpreted as absence of circulation. Panama is among the best-characterized Central American systems. Surveillance during 1999–2019 defined an endemic area encompassing approximately 27% of Panama’s national territory, not 27% of districts or cases; this mapped area does not exclude circulation elsewhere. Choclo virus (CHOV) is associated with the reservoir Oligoryzomys costaricensis, the Costa Rican pygmy rice rat; earlier Panamanian reports assigned this host to Oligoryzomys fulvescens, which accounts for the divergence between earlier and current nomenclature rather than indicating two distinct reservoirs. Systematic rodent sampling at more than 150 sites across Panama has since characterized this host, with overall hantavirus seroprevalence above 15% in the pygmy rice rat and seropositive animals concentrated in central-western Panama, where human CHOV incidence is also highest. Recognition of both HCPS and hantavirus fever increased following the introduction of decentralized testing and standardized surveillance, although such programmatic observations do not isolate the effects of individual health-system changes. South America contains multiple virus–host systems, including ANDV in the southern Andes, Juquitiba virus associated with Oligoryzomys nigripes, and Araraquara virus associated with Necromys lasiurus in Brazil. The recognized range extends to the Guiana Shield, where Maripa virus has been confirmed as a cause of HCPS in a documented case series from French Guiana. Reports from Bolivia, Peru, and northern Argentina continue to extend both the geographic range and the inventory of implicated viruses, including HCPS in Santa Cruz and Tarija, Rio Mamoré virus endemicity in the Peruvian Amazon, and a newly described orthohantavirus associated with HCPS in northern Argentina; a narrative synthesis of rodent hosts and genotypes in southern South America describes the corresponding host–virus associations. Host composition, landscape structure, and longitudinal reservoir dynamics may affect local spillover probability, but these relationships cannot be translated into uniform continental incidence estimates. Epidemiologic and genomic investigations document limited person-to-person ANDV transmission in some close-contact settings. Human and reservoir data remain much less complete for several countries and for culturally distinct communities within countries. Reservoir infection is commonly persistent and clinically inapparent, allowing viral maintenance without obvious disease in the host population. Demography, movement, aggressive encounters, and density can alter transmission within reservoir populations, while local extinction and reintroduction can produce temporally unstable foci. These features mean that a single cross-sectional rodent survey provides only a snapshot of a dynamic system. The regional inventory in Supplementary Table S5 makes this asymmetry explicit: evidence is comparatively rich for SNV in the United States, CHOV in Panama, ANDV in Chile and Argentina, and several Brazilian systems, but is less detailed for much of Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean, and several countries in northern South America. These categories describe the sources used in this review, not verified absence of infection elsewhere. 4. Environmental and Socioecological Pathways of Exposure Climate affects hantavirus risk indirectly through ecological processes rather than through a uniform, linear relationship with human incidence. In arid and semi-arid systems, increased precipitation can increase primary productivity and food availability, followed by growth in reservoir populations and greater opportunities for human contact. Across Latin America and the Caribbean, however, the direction and magnitude of associations with precipitation and temperature vary among settings, reflecting differences in reservoir species, seasonality, land use, and human behavior. In northwestern Argentina, synchronous increases in rodent abundance have preceded HCPS activity, consistent with the value of longitudinal ecological monitoring while also illustrating the need for local calibration. Land-use change can modify both reservoir communities and human exposure. Forest fragmentation, agricultural expansion, and habitat conversion may favor generalist rodents in some landscapes and increase the frequency with which people work or live near reservoir habitat. Studies from Brazil have linked landscape configuration, sugarcane expansion, climate, and social variables with modeled or observed hantavirus risk, but the effects are context-dependent and should not be generalized as universal consequences of deforestation or warming. A systematic review of land-cover and land-use exposures likewise reported heterogeneous, setting-specific associations with human hantavirus infection risk rather than a consistent directional effect. At the point of contact, occupation and housing shape whether ecological hazard becomes individual exposure. Agricultural and forestry work, entry into poorly ventilated structures, sweeping or cleaning rodent-contaminated spaces, grain handling, and peridomestic rodent activity can increase contact with infectious urine, feces, or saliva. A systematic review found measurable hantavirus seroprevalence among agricultural and forestry workers, while case investigations in the United States have repeatedly identified household and occupational settings as plausible exposure sites. Exposure prevention is therefore not reducible to knowledge alone. In an endemic community in Panama, preventive practices were associated with perceived barriers, education, and community experience of disease; the authors argued for community-based interventions that address practical obstacles rather than relying exclusively on information campaigns. These findings are important for equity: recommendations that require structural housing repairs, specialized protective equipment, or changes in livelihood may be biologically reasonable but difficult to implement without material support. Across disciplines, the inference is uneven. Longitudinal ecological observations and geographically explicit modeling can associate reservoir dynamics with environmental conditions, but usually do not measure the infectious dose received by individual people. Occupational investigations more directly identify contact opportunities; however, links from such exposure to early immune control or eventual mortality remain rarely measured within the same population. Accordingly, each proposed transition should be tested rather than treated as a proven causal chain (Supplementary Table S6). Figure 1 depicts an explicitly hypothesized pathway from ecological change to recognized clinical outcomes; Supplementary Table S6 identifies the type of evidence and measurable indicator for each proposed link. The climatic and landscape associations are setting-specific, while diagnostic delay and critical-care capacity are proposed modifiers that have not been shown to explain regional mortality differences independently. 5. From Exposure to Infection: Viral Entry and Early Host Response Human infection most often follows inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with rodent excreta, although direct contact with contaminated material and, less commonly, bites can also provide routes of exposure. ANDV adds a distinct pathway because close-contact person-to-person transmission is documented, including household and nosocomial clusters. The existence of these routes does not imply that every exposure produces infection: inhaled dose, environmental stability, route of entry, viral genotype, and host factors all influence whether productive infection is established. Protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been identified experimentally as an essential entry factor for ANDV and SNV in the tested cellular and animal systems. This result supports a specific virus–host interaction; it does not establish a PCDH1 requirement for every New World orthohantavirus or explain interindividual variation in clinical severity. The relative importance of entry co-factors and tissue-specific susceptibility remains unresolved. Vascular endothelial cells are central to HCPS pathology, but infection is largely non-cytolytic. Endothelial infection therefore differs from diseases in which extensive direct cell destruction explains organ failure. full_text_sections.full_text: Hantavirus at the Climate–Rodent–Human Interface: Integrating Immunopathogenesis, Ecological Drivers, and Health Inequities in the Americas New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) within heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings across the Americas. This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement. 1. Introduction New World orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a rapidly progressive illness characterized by capillary leak, pulmonary edema, shock, and, in severe cases, cardiorespiratory failure. The syndrome was recognized internationally after the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States, and subsequent surveillance established a heterogeneous distribution of pathogenic orthohantaviruses across North, Central, and South America. Although HCPS is uncommon compared with many endemic infections, case fatality remains substantial and varies by virus, setting, clinical recognition, and access to supportive care. The major New World viruses illustrate why a single continental model is inadequate. Sin Nombre virus (SNV) predominates among recognized cases in the United States, Andes virus (ANDV) is a major cause of HCPS in Argentina and Chile and can be transmitted from person to person, and Choclo virus (CHOV) sustains endemic transmission in Panama. South America also contains extensive viral and reservoir diversity, including Juquitiba- and Araraquara-associated transmission systems in Brazil. This diversity affects reservoir ecology, transmission opportunities, immune interactions, and the design of surveillance systems. Hantavirus risk is usually described through the climate–rodent–human interface. Climatic variability and landscape change influence vegetation and food availability, which can alter reservoir abundance and movement; housing, occupation, and human behavior then shape whether infected rodents and people share the same spaces. That ecological pathway is necessary but incomplete. Exposure does not invariably produce infection, and infection does not invariably progress to severe HCPS. The transition from infection to clinical disease depends on viral entry, innate sensing and immune evasion, endothelial barrier regulation, cellular immune responses, and humoral immunity. The final transition, from clinically apparent infection to a documented outcome, also depends on case ascertainment and care pathways. Early HCPS symptoms are nonspecific, confirmatory assays and referral services vary across settings, and severe disease may require specialized critical care. These conditions plausibly affect recognition and management, although available comparative studies do not quantify their independent contribution to differences in case fatality. Serosurveys from particular Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous geographic and exposure contexts; they do not support assumptions of ethnicity-based intrinsic biological susceptibility. This review examines how ecological exposure, host immune responses, and structural conditions may be connected along a mechanism-to-population continuum, with emphasis on settings for which primary human and reservoir evidence is available. Its purpose is to identify supported links and explicitly distinguish them from cross-level hypotheses that require prospective testing. 2. Methodology We conducted a critical narrative review integrating clinical, epidemiological, ecological, and mechanistic evidence on New World orthohantaviruses in the Americas within a One Health framework. The literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos, and LILACS, from database inception through 29 September 2026, without language restrictions. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH/DeCS), where applicable, and free-text terms adapted to each database, covering hantaviruses and relevant New World viruses, reservoir ecology, climate, land use, transmission, immunopathogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, clinical management, surveillance, and structural determinants of health (Supplementary Tables S1–S4). The PubMed/MEDLINE search was updated on 27 October 2026. Additional relevant publications were identified through reference-list screening. Institutional public-health reports and peer-reviewed surveillance studies were selected based on source credibility, geographic relevance, temporal coverage, and traceability to provide complementary context on regional epidemiological patterns, surveillance activities, and public-health responses. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts, and potentially relevant full texts, resolving disagreements through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Publications were selected based on relevance, directness of evidence, and contextual applicability. Priority was given to clinical and epidemiological investigations, reservoir and environmental studies, and experimental research with mechanistic relevance. Relevant reviews and reports from recognized national or regional public-health institutions were also considered. Publications with limited thematic relevance, insufficiently supported findings, or unclear geographic or ecological applicability were not prioritized. Seventy-six sources are cited in this review. Relevant information was extracted on study design, geographic setting, viral species, study population or ecological context, principal findings, and methodological limitations. Evidence was organized and synthesized thematically, considering consistency across studies, directness of findings, and inferential limitations. Experimental evidence, observational associations, and proposed mechanistic or population-level relationships were distinguished during interpretation. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or certainty-of-evidence grading was performed for individual studies. The Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) informed the scientific reasoning, referencing, and presentation of the review (Supplementary Table S8). Figures were prepared using BioRender, including its integrated generative artificial intelligence tools. 3. Main directions: The review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Current state: Evidence is uneven, focused mainly on the US, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Gaps: Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central, yet cytokine, NK‑cell, and antibody Fc links to outcomes remain unproven and lack prognostic validation. papers.full_text: Hantavirus receptor recognition: From structural insights to therapeutic opportunities Hantavirus infections illustrate a persistent gap between advances in molecular virology and the availability of targeted clinical interventions. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV), cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which can progress rapidly to respiratory failure and shock. Old World hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), often involving acute kidney injury and vascular dysfunction. No vaccine is licensed for HCPS, and no targeted antiviral treatment has established efficacy for hantavirus syndromes. Inactivated HFRS vaccines are used in parts of Asia, although their performance varies across settings. Early recognition and skilled supportive care therefore remain central to patient outcomes. Preventing infection before a virus enters its target cells offers an attractive therapeutic opportunity. For many viruses, protective antibodies work by blocking attachment or membrane fusion. In 2018, we identified protocadherin‐1 (PCDH1) as a critical entry receptor for ANDV and SNV, including in human endothelial cells, which are major targets of hantavirus infection. Subsequent studies showed that direct engagement of PCDH1 is important for ANDV pathogenesis in a Syrian hamster model. Yet a fundamental question remained: how does the assembled hantavirus spike recognize this receptor? Our recent study in Nature resolves this interaction at near‐atomic resolution. Rather than binding an individual glycoprotein subunit, a single PCDH1 molecule engages a deep central cavity formed by four Gn subunits of the Gn–Gc spike. Complementary structural, functional, and large‐scale mutational analyses identified regions of Gn critical for receptor recognition. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for developing strategies to prevent hantavirus entry (Table 1). Translational opportunities arising from the structural and functional characterization of hantavirus receptor recognition. Area Key findings and implications Priorities for translation Therapeutic antibodies Neutralizing antibodies block receptor engagement through distinct mechanisms, supporting the development of antibodies with complementary activities. Evaluate neutralization breadth, resistance, and therapeutic efficacy after infection. Entry inhibitors Defining the PCDH1‐binding interface provides opportunities to develop engineered binding proteins, receptor mimetics, and small‐molecule inhibitors Identify and evaluate candidates for antiviral potency, specificity, and safety. Vaccine development Structural insights into Gn–Gc organization in the context of receptor binding and antibody recognition could inform the design of immunogens that elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies Assess the breadth, durability, and protective efficacy of vaccine‐induced responses. Antiviral resistance Functional mapping of receptor‐binding determinants can identify regions of the viral spike that are less tolerant of mutations Define potential escape pathways and their effects on viral entry and fitness Broad‐spectrum countermeasures The possibility of analogous receptor‐binding sites in divergent hantaviruses raises opportunities for identifying shared therapeutic targets Establish receptor usage in Old World hantaviruses and assess conservation of the binding surface One immediate implication concerns therapeutic antibodies. A recessed receptor‐binding pocket might seem largely inaccessible to conventional antibodies. Nevertheless, our work explains how different potent neutralizing antibodies interfere with PCDH1 engagement. ANDV‐5 and MIB22 bind near the opening of the central cavity and directly block access to the PCDH1‐binding site, whereas ADI‐65534 and ANDV‐34 bind more peripheral epitopes and prevent receptor engagement through steric interference mediated by their antibody constant regions. Thus, an antibody need not bind the deepest part of a receptor pocket to block an essential entry event. This distinction provides a rationale for evaluating antibodies that recognize accessible, non‐overlapping surfaces and for considering combinations with complementary mechanisms. The therapeutic potential of neutralizing antibodies is supported by studies demonstrating post‐exposure protection against lethal ANDV infection in Syrian hamsters, using an MIB22‐containing antibody cocktail and the engineered broadly neutralizing antibody ADI‐65534, although clinical efficacy remains unproven. A second opportunity is to develop agents that interrupt the virus‐receptor interface without using conventional antibodies. Smaller antibody formats, including single‐domain antibodies, could potentially approach recessed surfaces that are difficult for larger molecules to access. Soluble receptor mimetics or other engineered binding proteins offer additional conceptual routes to prevent attachment. The structure also supplies a starting point for evaluating whether the pocket or its surrounding surfaces can be targeted by small molecules. These approaches will require further investigation to determine whether they can safely and effectively block viral infection. Spike‐directed agents may also have advantages over broadly disrupting PCDH1 itself, which has normal functions in host tissues. Beyond blocking receptor engagement, understanding the architecture of the hantavirus spike could also guide the development of more effective countermeasures. For several important human viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, stabilizing viral surface proteins in their prefusion state has been instrumental in developing vaccines that elicit potent neutralizing antibodies. Encouragingly, a recent study demonstrated that a prefusion‐stabilized Hantaan virus glycoprotein vaccine enhanced neutralizing antibody responses and reduced viral burdens in mice. Our findings could inform similar vaccine‐design strategies against HCPS‐causing viruses. Moreover, identifying ways to prevent the structural changes required for viral entry could reveal additional targets for antiviral development. Two important uncertainties remain. First, even conserved entry interfaces may tolerate changes that reduce inhibitor binding while retaining sufficient viral function. The development of scalable entry systems and deep mutational profiling approaches, as demonstrated in our study, provides an opportunity to systematically define the functional constraints governing receptor recognition. Extending such approaches to antibody escape, entry competence, and fusion could help identify vulnerable regions of the spike, anticipate resistance pathways, and guide the selection of therapeutic targets. Second, PCDH1 is not an established receptor for the Old World hantaviruses responsible for HFRS. Nevertheless, the corresponding central cavity of their glycoprotein spikes might serve as a binding site for unidentified receptors. If confirmed, this could reveal a shared vulnerability across divergent hantaviruses and provide opportunities for developing broadly acting therapeutics against both HCPS‐ and HFRS‐causing viruses. Promising candidates will need to demonstrate activity against phylogenetically distinct viruses, an acceptable safety profile, and benefit in appropriate preclinical models, including when treatment begins after infection. An important clinical question is whether blocking entry remains beneficial after symptom onset, when host inflammatory responses and vascular injury may already be established. The limited availability of animal models that reproduce human disease and the specialized containment required for studies with pathogenic hantaviruses remain significant practical obstacles. Our findings provide a structural and functional framework for developing new antibody‐based therapeutics, entry inhibitors, and improved vaccine strategies against pathogenic hantaviruses. CONFLICT OF INTEREST STATEMENT Rohit K. Jangra is a co‐inventor on a U.S. patent covering methods and assays for treating hantavirus infections. REFERENCES Andes virus — a clinical review The protective efficacy of inactivated vaccine against hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: a meta‐analysis Protocadherin‐1 is essential for cell entry by New World Hantaviruses Two point mutations in protocadherin‐1 disrupt hantavirus recognition and afford protection against lethal infection Structural basis for protocadherin‐1 recognition by New World hantaviruses Therapeutic efficacy of human monoclonal antibodies against Andes virus infection in Syrian Hamsters Structural and mechanistic basis of neutralization by a pan‐hantavirus protective antibody Prefusion‐stabilized Hantaan virus glycoprotein nucleic acid vaccine elicits potent neutralizing antibody responses via germinal center activation

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause severe diseases such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) (F2, F3) and there are no licensed vaccines for HCPS and no proven antiviral therapy (F4), highlighting a gap between molecular knowledge and clinical tools (F1).
analysis.methods: The authors performed near‑atomic resolution structural determination of the hantavirus Gn‑Gc spike bound to the entry receptor protocadherin‑1, complemented by functional assays and large‑scale mutational analyses to map receptor‑binding determinants (F12‑F15).
analysis.results: A single PCDH1 molecule engages a deep central cavity formed by four Gn subunits (F13), and mutational mapping identified Gn regions essential for this interaction (F14). Neutralizing antibodies block receptor engagement by either occluding the cavity entrance (ANDV‑5, MIB22) or steric hindrance from peripheral epitopes (ADI‑65534, ANDV‑34) (F24‑F26), and antibody cocktails protected Syrian hamsters from lethal ANDV infection, though clinical efficacy is unproven (F27).
analysis.contribution: These findings provide a molecular framework for developing entry inhibitors, therapeutic antibodies, engineered binding proteins, and prefusion‑stabilized vaccine immunogens, offering multiple translational avenues against hantaviruses (F16‑F21, F36).
analysis.limitations: The protective effect of antibodies has only been demonstrated in a Syrian hamster model, and clinical efficacy in humans remains unproven (F27); further investigation is needed to assess safety and effectiveness of proposed therapeutics (F32).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus diseases like HCPS and HFRS lack licensed vaccines and proven antivirals, creating a gap between molecular insights and clinical tools. Methods: Near‑atomic structural analysis of the Gn‑Gc spike with PCDH1, plus functional and mutational studies, defined the receptor‑binding interface. Results: PCDH1 binds a central cavity formed by four Gn subunits; key Gn residues were mapped, and distinct neutralizing antibodies block entry by cavity occlusion or steric hindrance, protecting hamsters but not yet proven in humans. Contribution: The work offers a structural basis for entry inhibitors, antibody therapies, engineered proteins, and improved vaccine designs. Limitations: Efficacy demonstrated only in animal models; human clinical benefit remains unproven and further safety/efficacy studies are required.

papers.title: Ecological Correlates and Spatiotemporal Trends of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in West Kazakhstan: A 25-Year One Health Surveillance Study (2001-2025).
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis of public health concern in West Kazakhstan, yet long-term studies linking human and reservoir surveillance are scarce. We analyzed laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases (2001-2025) and routine rodent surveillance data from five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region within a One Health framework. Associations were estimated using negative binomial regression with district fixed effects and year-clustered robust standard errors (2002-2024; 115 district-years). Overall, 314 cases were recorded (81.2% male), with a major outbreak in 2005 (85 cases) and a resurgence in 2024-2025 (27 and 41 cases). Burlinsky District reported the most cases (44.9%), whereas Baiterek District had the highest incidence in 2016-2025. Of 132,694 rodents examined, 1083 (0.82%) were hantavirus antigen-positive. A larger share of the annual Mus musculus catch obtained in spring-summer was associated with higher case counts (incidence rate ratio 1.051 per percentage point; 95% CI: 1.024-1.080), and this was robust to excluding outbreak years. The number of positive rodents was associated with cases, but not after standardization for sampling effort. These associations do not establish M. musculus as a reservoir and are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, increased peridomestic exposure.

papers.full_text: Ecological Correlates and Spatiotemporal Trends of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in West Kazakhstan: A 25-Year One Health Surveillance Study (2001–2025) Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis of public health concern in West Kazakhstan, yet long-term studies linking human and reservoir surveillance are scarce. We analyzed laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases (2001–2025) and routine rodent surveillance data from five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region within a One Health framework. Associations were estimated using negative binomial regression with district fixed effects and year-clustered robust standard errors (2002–2024; 115 district-years). Overall, 314 cases were recorded (81.2% male), with a major outbreak in 2005 (85 cases) and a resurgence in 2024–2025 (27 and 41 cases). Burlinsky District reported the most cases (44.9%), whereas Baiterek District had the highest incidence in 2016–2025. Of 132,694 rodents examined, 1083 (0.82%) were hantavirus antigen-positive. A larger share of the annual Mus musculus catch obtained in spring–summer was associated with higher case counts (incidence rate ratio 1.051 per percentage point; 95% CI: 1.024–1.080), and this was robust to excluding outbreak years. The number of positive rodents was associated with cases, but not after standardization for sampling effort. These associations do not establish M. musculus as a reservoir and are consistent with, but do not demonstrate, increased peridomestic exposure. 1. Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonosis caused by orthohantaviruses. It is characterized by acute fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and renal dysfunction, and causes substantial morbidity and mortality across Eurasia. Although China reports most of the global HFRS burden, the disease remains an important problem in neighboring countries, including Russia and Kazakhstan. In West Kazakhstan, particularly in areas bordering the Russian Federation, HFRS persists as a public health concern because rural and peri-urban populations live in close proximity to natural foci of infection. The West Kazakhstan Region is the only officially recognized HFRS-endemic region of Kazakhstan with registered human cases. The first case was detected in 2000, and natural foci of orthohantaviruses have been described in its northern districts. HFRS transmission is shaped by interacting ecological factors, including reservoir population density, environmental conditions, and anthropogenic land-use change. Rodent species occupy distinct niches, including woodland, open steppe, and peridomestic structures, and their distribution influences where and how often humans are exposed. Climate and humidity affect food availability for rodents and the environmental persistence of virus shed in excreta, which is the main source of human infection by inhalation. Agricultural expansion and landscape features that increase human–rodent contact further raise the probability of spillover. Most epidemiological studies of HFRS have focused on outbreak investigations or short-term trends. Voutilainen et al. showed that intensive forest management altered Puumala orthohantavirus infection in boreal bank vole populations, and Zhang et al. identified environmental and meteorological factors associated with HFRS incidence in Weifang, China. Long-term studies that analyze human and reservoir surveillance data jointly remain concentrated in China and Russia, and comparable evidence from other endemic regions, including Kazakhstan, is limited. Linking human epidemiological trends with reservoir ecology over long periods can help public health authorities assess risk in endemic areas. This study applied a One Health framework, integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance data. Our objectives were to describe the spatiotemporal distribution of HFRS in five districts of the West Kazakhstan Region over 2001–2025, and to quantify associations between human HFRS case counts and reservoir indicators (the seasonal distribution of rodent captures by species, rodent hantavirus positivity, and human seroprevalence), while accounting for time-invariant differences between districts. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design, Area, and Periods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal ecological study in five administrative units of the West Kazakhstan Region: Burlinsky, Baiterek, Chingirlau, and Terekty districts and Uralsk City (Table 1; Figure 1). Human case data are described for the full period 2001–2025. Inferential analyses were restricted to 2002–2024 (5 districts × 23 years = 115 district-years) because no spring–summer rodent trapping was performed in 2001 and spring–summer rodent data for 2025 were not yet available at the time of analysis. 2.2. Human Case Data and Case Definition Data on all HFRS cases registered from 2001 to 2025 were obtained from the Ural Anti-Plague Station. Each record included year, district of residence, and sex. A case was defined as a patient with a clinically compatible illness and laboratory confirmation according to the national clinical protocols in force at the time, most recently the Clinical Protocol for Diagnosis and Treatment of HFRS of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Kazakhstan (29 March 2019, Protocol No. 60), which defines serological confirmation as a fourfold or greater rise in antibody titer in paired sera collected 10–12 days apart. Laboratory confirmation was performed at the laboratory of the Ural Anti-Plague Station by detection of hantavirus-specific IgM antibodies and/or a fourfold or greater rise in IgG antibody titer by ELISA, using the “VectoHanta-IgM” and “VectoHanta-IgG” test systems (JSC Vector-Best, Novosibirsk, Russia). Molecular testing (RT-PCR) was not performed, so the infecting orthohantavirus species was not determined. Testing of patients for leptospirosis was not systematically recorded. District population estimates were obtained from the Bureau of National Statistics of the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2016–2025. District incidence was therefore calculated for 2016–2025 only. Regional incidence was calculated using the total population of the West Kazakhstan Region. Because the official 2025 regional estimate was not yet available, the 2025 regional incidence was estimated using the 2024 population. 2.3. Rodent Surveillance Rodent monitoring was conducted by the Ural Anti-Plague Station as part of routine zoonotic surveillance at 49–50 fixed sites in the study area, located in natural habitats (riparian forest, steppe, and fields) and within or adjacent to settlements. Surveys were conducted twice yearly, in spring–summer (May–August) and autumn–winter (October–January). Rodents were captured with Gero snap traps and live traps (box and mesh traps) baited with black bread soaked in unrefined sunflower oil, with approximately 500–1000 trap-nights per season. Exact trap-night totals were not available. Between 2001 and 2025, 132,694 rodents were examined (47,042 in spring–summer and 85,652 in autumn–winter; Table 2). Species were identified by trained zoologists on the basis of external morphology and cranial and dental characters using standard identification keys. Four species were analyzed: the bank vole (Myodes glareolus), the common vole (Microtus arvalis), the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), and the house mouse (Mus musculus). For each species and year, the seasonal distribution of captures was expressed as the percentage of that year’s captures of the species obtained in spring–summer. The autumn–winter value is its complement (100% minus the spring–summer value). This indicator describes the seasonal timing of captures within each species. It is not the species’ share of the rodent community and not a measure of absolute abundance. Rodents were tested for hantavirus antigen in lung tissue by ELISA using the “Hantagnost” test system (M.P. Chumakov Federal Scientific Center for Research and Development of Immunobiological Preparations of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Institute of Poliomyelitis, Moscow, Russia). Rodent positivity was recorded as the annual number of antigen-positive animals and, for sensitivity analysis, as the percentage of positive animals among all rodents examined in that year. Rodents, including M. musculus, were not typed for hantaviruses by RT-PCR or sequencing. Rodents were also tested for Leptospira by PCR using the “AmpliSens” assay (Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, Moscow, Russia). Rodent indicators were available only at the regional level. The same annual values were therefore assigned to all five districts. 2.4. Human Seroprevalence Human hantavirus seroprevalence (“population immunity”) was measured in serological surveys of adult residents of HFRS-risk areas, conducted by the laboratory of the Ural Anti-Plague Station over 10 years (2006, 2007, 2009, 2011–2014, 2016, 2024, and 2025). In each survey, 72–333 adult residents were tested for hantavirus-specific IgG antibodies by ELISA using the “VectoHanta-IgG” test system (JSC Vector-Best, Novosibirsk, Russia). In total, 1799 persons were tested. Seroprevalence was calculated as the percentage of IgG-positive persons among those tested. 2.5. Statistical Analysis Variables are summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD), median (range), or n (%). Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between district-level annual case counts and the rodent indicators (n = 115 district-years). Because human seroprevalence was available for only 10 years, its correlation with annual regional case counts was assessed at the year level. Because the outcome is an overdispersed count, the primary model was negative binomial (NB2) regression with a log link and district fixed effects (Baiterek District as the reference), with the seasonal distribution of M. musculus captures and the number of antigen-positive rodents as predictors. Other species were not retained because they showed no association in bivariate analysis. Overdispersion was assessed with the Pearson χ2/df of the corresponding Poisson model and a likelihood-ratio test of the NB dispersion parameter (α = 0). Because the rodent predictors vary only between years, standard errors were clustered by year (23 clusters). No population offset was used because district populations were not available before 2016. The district fixed effects absorb stable differences in population size between districts. Results are reported as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). To address the specification of the panel model, we also fitted a linear model and compared pooled ordinary least squares (OLS), random-effects (RE), and fixed-effects (FE) specifications. District heterogeneity was assessed with an F-test of district effects (FE vs. pooled OLS) and the Breusch–Pagan Lagrange multiplier test (RE vs. pooled OLS). A Hausman test (FE vs. RE) could not be meaningfully computed because the predictors take identical values for all districts in a given year. They therefore have no between-district variation, and the FE, RE, and pooled OLS slope estimates are identical. Serial correlation was assessed with the Wooldridge test, groupwise heteroskedasticity with the modified Wald test, and multicollinearity with variance inflation factors (VIFs). These diagnostics were used to justify the choice of the count model as the primary analysis. Four sensitivity analyses were conducted. The primary model was refitted after excluding 2024, the year with the most extreme spring–summer M. musculus value, and after excluding the 2005 outbreak year. It was also refitted with the percentage of positive rodents among those examined in place of the number of positive rodents, to account for sampling effort, and at the regional year level (n = 23). Analyses were performed in Stata version 16 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). A p-value < 0.05 was considered significant. A generative artificial intelligence tool (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA) was used to assist with the re-analysis of the surveillance data, including writing analysis code, computing preliminary estimates, and preparing Figure 2 and Figure 3. All estimates reported in this manuscript were reproduced independently by the authors in Stata, and the authors verified all figures against the source data. 2.6. Ethical Considerations The study used anonymized, aggregated surveillance data. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of West Kazakhstan Marat Ospanov Medical University (approval No. 12-2025/180-HC, 26 December 2025). 3. Results 3.1. Epidemiological and Demographic Characteristics From 2001 to 2025, 314 laboratory-confirmed HFRS cases were recorded in the five study units, a mean of 12.6 ± 18.4 cases per year (median 6; range 0–85). Most cases occurred in males (255; 81.2%) (Table 3). Case numbers fluctuated markedly (Figure 2). The largest outbreak occurred in 2005 (85 cases), followed by smaller peaks in 2003 (20), 2006 (20), and 2008 (30). After very low numbers in 2019–2023 (0–3 cases per year), cases rose sharply in 2024 (27) and 2025 (41). Regional incidence ranged from 0 to 1.70 per 100,000 in 2016–2023, increased to 3.88 per 100,000 in 2024, and reached an estimated 5.89 per 100,000 in 2025. Burlinsky District accounted for 44.9% of all cases and Baiterek District for 31.2% (Table 4), largely because of the 2005 outbreak, during which Burlinsky reported 54 cases. In the period with population data (2016–2025), however, Baiterek had the highest cumulative incidence (63.8 per 100,000), followed by Burlinsky (33.5), Chingirlau (14.3), Uralsk City (10.2), and Terekty (5.2). The resurgence in 2024–2025 was concentrated in Baiterek (22.7 and 22.2 per 100,000) and Burlinsky (12.2 and 15.8 per 100,000), with a rise in Uralsk City in 2025 (16 cases; 4.3 per 100,000). The single-year peak in Chingirlau (13.5 per 100,000 in 2017) reflected 2 cases in a small population (Figure 3). 3.2. Rodent Surveillance and Correlation Analysis The number of rodents examined per year ranged from 74 (2001) to 11,561 (2012) and was 1755 in 2024. Rodent hantavirus positivity declined from 1.95% in 2001–2005 to 0.18% in 2021–2025 (Table 2), including in 2024–2025, when human cases increased. For all four species, most captures occurred in autumn–winter (Figure S1). In 2002–2024, the mean percentage of annual captures obtained in spring–summer was 30.4% (range 7.0–59.3%) for M. glareolus, 42.2% (19.6–64.6%) for M. arvalis, 38.1% (21.0–61.5%) for A. uralensis, and 32.6% (10.6–69.1%) for M. musculus. In 2023 and 2024, spring–summer captures accounted for only 7.0% and 8.6% of annual M. glareolus captures. In contrast, 2024 was the only year in which most M. musculus captures (69.1%) occurred in spring–summer. The spring–summer percentage of M. musculus captures was positively correlated with district-level case counts (r = 0.32, p < 0.001; Table 5). The autumn–winter value is its complement and therefore shows the same coefficient with the opposite sign. The spring–summer percentages of the other species, including the bank vole, were not correlated with case counts. The number of antigen-positive rodents showed a weak, non-significant positive correlation (r = 0.18, p = 0.058). At the year level, human seroprevalence was not significantly correlated with case counts (r = −0.26, p = 0.50, n = 9 surveys in 2006–2024; r = 0.47, p = 0.17, n = 10 including 2025, when 41 of 150 persons tested were seropositive). 3.3. Regression Analysis Case counts were strongly overdispersed (mean 2.37, variance 36.6 per district-year; Poisson Pearson χ2/df = 4.08), and the NB dispersion parameter differed significantly from zero (α = 0.97; likelihood-ratio χ2 = 152.2, p < 0.001). In the linear panel specification, district effects were significant (F(4, 108) = 4.17, p = 0.003) and the Breusch–Pagan LM test indicated unobserved district heterogeneity (χ2 = 11.29, p < 0.001). There was no evidence of first-order serial correlation (Wooldridge F(1, 4) = 1.23, p = 0.33), but strong groupwise heteroskedasticity was present (modified Wald χ2(5) = 1227, p < 0.001), driven mainly by the large residual variance in Burlinsky District. Multicollinearity was negligible (VIF = 1.05) (Table 6). These results supported a count model with district fixed effects and robust standard errors as the primary analysis. In the primary NB model (Table 7), each one-percentage-point increase in the share of annual M. musculus captures obtained in spring–summer was associated with a 5.1% higher expected case count (IRR = 1.051; 95% CI: 1.024–1.080; p < 0.001). Each additional antigen-positive rodent was associated with a 0.9% higher expected count (IRR = 1.009; 95% CI: 1.003–1.016; p = 0.004). After adjustment, Burlinsky District did not differ significantly from Baiterek (IRR = 1.33; 95% CI: 0.76–2.35), whereas Uralsk City (IRR = 0.60), Chingirlau (IRR = 0.16), and Terekty (IRR = 0.04) had significantly lower case counts. The linear FE model gave consistent results (β for M. musculus = 0.129 additional cases per district-year per percentage point; 95% CI with year-clustered SEs: 0.014–0.245; p = 0.030) (Table S1). The model did not reproduce the magnitude of outbreak peaks (fitted 18.3 vs. 85 observed cases in 2005), indicating that other, unmeasured factors contributed to outbreak size. The association with M. musculus was robust in all sensitivity analyses (Table 8). In contrast, the association with rodent positivity disappeared when it was expressed as a percentage of rodents examined (IRR = 1.33 per percentage point; 95% CI: 0.56–3.13; p = 0.52), indicating that the association with the absolute number of positive animals largely reflected sampling effort. 4. papers.title_zh: 西哈萨克斯坦 肾综合征出血热 的生态相关因素与时空趋势:一项跨越25年的 One Health 监测研究(2001-2025)

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种在哈萨克斯坦西部受到公共卫生关注的啮齿动物传播的人畜共患病,但将人类与宿主监测联系起来的长期研究仍然稀缺。
analysis_zh.methods: 对哈萨克斯坦西部地区五个区实验室确诊的肾综合征出血热病例(2001‐2025)及常规啮齿动物监测数据进行回顾性纵向生态学研究,采用负二项回归,加入地区固定效应和按年份聚类的稳健标准误(2002‐2024;115个地区‐年)。
analysis_zh.results: 共记录314例(男性占81.2%),其中2005年出现大规模暴发(85例),2024‐2025年出现复发(分别为27例和41例)。Burlinsky 区报告的病例最多(占44.9%),而 Baiterek 区在2016‐2025年发病率最高。共检查132,694只啮齿动物,其中1083只(0.82%)为 汉坦病毒 抗原阳性。春夏季捕获的 Mus musculus 年度比例较大与病例数增加相关(IRR 每个百分点 1.051;95% CI 1.024‐1.080),该关联在排除暴发年份后仍稳健;阳性啮齿动物数量与病例数呈正相关,但在对采样努力标准化后不再显著。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究采用 One Health 框架,整合人类、动物和环境监测数据,首次提供哈萨克斯坦西部地区长期、区级的肾综合征出血热生态关联,为风险评估和公共卫生干预提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 关联性分析并不证明因果关系,也未确认 Mus musculus 为宿主;阳性啮齿动物计数的采样努力未标准化;由于数据缺失,分析仅限于2002‐2024年,且仅研究了五个区。

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective.
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges. papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10 , STAT1 , and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1 , BCL2 , and STAT 3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2 , MAPK3 , and TNF . Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host-pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the "One Health" framework.
