papers.full_text: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization Simple Summary Hantaan virus, carried by rodents, causes severe bleeding and kidney disease in humans, making it a key concern for veterinary wildlife surveillance. Using computational methods, we studied early viral effects on human cells and screened for natural compounds. Three immune genes, CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10, were strongly activated early. Among six compounds, quercetin was most promising, with predicted good absorption and low toxicity. Further analysis indicated that quercetin may promote cell viability and suppress inflammation, thereby protecting cells from damage induced by HTNV infection. In baseline pharmacological assays using uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin at 3.9–7.8 μM was non-toxic, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted quercetin binds to the viral RNA polymerase at Lys884 and Arg892. These findings propose quercetin as a computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses. Abstract Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses, enveloped segmented negative-sense RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. They are predominantly maintained in rodent reservoir species, with which they have co-evolved a persistent, typically asymptomatic infection. Infected rodents do not manifest overt disease but sustain long-term viral carriage, with continuous shedding of infectious particles via excretory routes, namely urine, feces, and saliva. Human infection occurs through inhalation of virus-contaminated aerosols, direct contact with contaminated fomites or wounds, or, less frequently, via the digestive tract, leading to two severe clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS). Orthohantavirus hantaanense (Hantaan virus, HTNV) is the predominant etiological agent of HFRS in Asia, with reported case-fatality rates approaching 15%. Importantly, the occurrence of HTNV infection is not determined solely by viral or host factors. Human exposure is closely associated with the abundance, distribution, and infection status of rodent hosts, as well as the frequency of human–rodent contact. Rodent population dynamics and virus shedding are further influenced by environmental and ecological conditions, including climate variability, habitat characteristics, agricultural activities, and food availability and storage. Consequently, HTNV represents a typical One Health-related challenge in which viral maintenance in animals, environmental contamination, and human exposure are interconnected. Currently, no approved drug is available to break the aforementioned connection. Moreover, the clinical management of HTNV-infected cases still relies mainly on supportive treatment. In previous reports, ribavirin, a broad-spectrum nucleoside analog, has shown antiviral activity against hantaviruses and has been used in certain clinical settings. However, its therapeutic utility is limited by treatment timing and adverse effects, including hemolytic anemia and other treatment-related complications. Addressing these problems requires a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of HTNV and the exploration of potential drug candidates. After HTNV infection, on one hand, its own encoded proteins, such as nucleocapsid protein (NP) and glycoprotein (Gn/Gc), can inhibit the production of type I interferons by targeting the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling pathway, thereby suppressing the early warning system of the host’s innate immunity. In addition, NP can recruit and interact with fatty acid synthase (FASN), regulating lipid synthesis activity, providing necessary metabolic support for viral replication. On the other hand, HTNV infection can also activate the HIF-1 signaling pathway, aggravating barrier dysfunction and vascular leakage. Clinical studies have confirmed that the earlier the intervention is carried out for HTNV infection, the higher the cure rate for the patients. Therefore, identifying the targets of the early interaction between HTNV and the host and using these targets to explore potential candidate drugs is an effective way to address the one health-related threats posed by HTNV. By integrating omics results, compound databases, and computer-aided drug design, a systematic framework has been established to elucidate the interactions between bioactive compounds and complex biological networks. The framework integrating omics and computational drug design can not only discover antiviral drugs that protect humans, but also the host pathways it reveals may provide clues for understanding the persistence mechanism of pathogens in rodents. From the perspective of One Health, this means that intervention strategies can simultaneously address both “reducing human cases” and “understanding the maintenance mechanism of rodents”. For instance, Msobo et al. combined LC–MS-based metabolomics with network pharmacology to investigate the anti-SARS-CoV-2 potential of Salvia aurea and Salvia dolomitica, thereby identifying 83 phytochemicals predicted to interact strongly with multiple SARS-CoV-2-associated targets. Accordingly, the present study adopted a target-oriented strategy that integrates bioinformatics, network pharmacology, and molecular docking, together with preliminary in vitro transcriptomic and cytotoxicity assessments in uninfected cells, to generate hypotheses regarding natural compounds capable of modulating HTNV-related host responses. The overall workflow is illustrated in Figure 1. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Cells and Compound The HEK293T cell line was acquired from the China Center for Type Culture Collection. Quercetin (purity, 99.80%) was purchased from MedChemExpress (Cat. No. HY-18085). Quercetin was dissolved in DMSO to a stock concentration of 200 mM and stored at −80 °C. The final DMSO concentration in cell culture medium did not exceed 0.1% (v/v), and an equivalent DMSO vehicle control was included in all experiments. 2.2. Prediction of Therapeutic Candidate for Early-Stage HTNV Infection HTNV-related host interaction targets were collected from disease-related public databases and the GEO database. For public database mining, HTNV-related targets were retrieved from OMIM (, accessed on 9 June 2026), GeneCards (, accessed on 9 June 2026), and MalaCards (, accessed on 9 June 2026) using the keyword “Hantavirus” with species restricted to Homo sapiens. For transcriptomic data, the GSE89950 dataset profiling digital gene expression (DGE) in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) at 24 h post-exposure to HTNV components was retrieved from the GEO database. This dataset included three conditions (Mock, HTNV, and HTNV [Co60]), with one sample per condition. The processed per-gene DGE statistics (expression values, fold changes, and p-values) were obtained from the supplementary DGE result files of the GEO series. To verify these statistics, we additionally downloaded the raw tag-level data of GSE89950 (GSE89950_RAW.tar: GSM2393958_Mock, GSM2393959_HTNV, and GSM2393960_Co60). Independent processing of the raw tag data yielded 96,272, 84,715, and 85,736 unique tags (corresponding to 3.43, 3.40, and 3.44 million copies) in the Mock, HTNV, and HTNV(Co60) samples, respectively. After gene-level summarization, a total of 12,503 expressed genes were obtained, identical to the union of the gene-level supplementary files; the gene-level count matrix was verified to be exactly consistent with the raw tag data. We then re-derived the differential expression statistics for both comparisons in R using an exact binomial test under the Poisson model, with library-size proportions as the null expectation. The independently derived statistics were highly concordant with the supplementary files, confirming the reliability of the DEG lists retrieved from GEO. Given the lack of biological replicates, DEG analysis was performed as an exploratory screening, and nominal p-values were reported without Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. DEGs were screened from the HTNV(Co60)_vs_Control and HTNV_vs_Control comparisons using thresholds of nominal p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0. Targets retrieved from public databases were imported into the STRING database () to construct a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, with a confidence score > 0.4 as the cutoff. Topological analysis was performed using the CytoNCA plugin in Cytoscape (version 3.9.1) to screen for core targets based on degree centrality (DC), betweenness centrality (BC), eigenvector centrality (EC), and closeness centrality (CC). Venn diagram analysis was used to identify the overlap between public database targets and DEGs from the HTNV (Co60)_vs_Control comparison. These core targets were then imported into the HERB database () for compound matching. Venn analysis was applied to the resulting compounds to screen for natural compounds predicted to interact with these core targets. 2.3. Prediction of Toxicity, Drug-Likeness, and Oral Bioavailability of Candidate Compounds SMILES notations for each compound were obtained from the PubChem database (, accessed on 1 July 2026). Organ toxicity (with 0.5 set as the threshold), toxicity endpoints, and metabolic characteristics were predicted using ProTox-II (, accessed on 20 June 2026). Interactions between each compound and six major cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4) were evaluated using a 0–1 scoring system. Drug-likeness (based on Lipinski, Ghose, Veber, Egan, and Muegge rules), bioavailability scores, and gastrointestinal (GI) absorption were predicted using SwissADME (, accessed on 20 June 2026). 2.4. Analysis of the Potential Targets of Quercetin in the Treatment of HTNV Infection Quercetin-related targets were retrieved from public databases [TCMSP (, accessed on 20 June 2026), SwissTargetPrediction (, accessed on 20 June 2026), and HERB (, accessed on 20 June 2026)] and the GEO database. The gene expression profiles of GSE167391 were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. This dataset included nine samples divided into three groups: normal control HUVECs (Control_1–3), ox-LDL-injured HUVECs (Ox_ldl_1–3), and quercetin-pretreated ox-LDL-injured HUVECs (Quercetin_1–3). Transcript-level FPKM values were aggregated to the gene level by summing isoforms, and genes with a mean FPKM ≥ 1 in at least one group (n = 3 per group) were retained. Because FPKM values are normalized continuous expression estimates that violate the count-based negative binomial assumption of DESeq2 and are likewise unsuitable for voom, the data were treated as microarray-like and analyzed with limma in R (v4.3.2). FPKM values were log2-transformed with a pseudocount of 1 and quantile-normalized. A linear model was fitted with the design~0 + group. Comparisons were made between Ox-ldl vs. Control and Quercetin_Ox-ldl vs. Control. Genes with an adjusted p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg) < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0 were considered differentially expressed. Venn analysis was then applied to intersect the DEGs from these comparisons with the quercetin-related targets, thereby identifying the potential targets of quercetin in the intervention against HTNV infection. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the targets was performed using the DAVID (, accessed on 20 August 2026). 2.5. Baseline Pharmacological Characterization of Candidate Compounds in Uninfected Cells To evaluate the potential of quercetin to protect cell proliferation, we integrated target data from online databases with quercetin-related targets identified from our transcriptomic analysis. A protein–protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using the STRING database, and four topological parameters, namely degree centrality (DC), betweenness centrality (BC), closeness centrality (CC), and eigenvector centrality (EC), were calculated with the CytoNCA plugin in Cytoscape 3.9.1. KEGG pathway and Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analyses were performed using DAVID (, accessed on 20 June 2026), and the enriched terms were ranked to identify the core functional pathways associated with the hub targets. Molecular docking of quercetin with the top-ranked targets was conducted using CB-Dock2 (, accessed on 22 July 2026). For in vitro validation, the initial concentration of quercetin was prepared at 1000 μM, and 10 concentration gradients were generated through a twofold dilution method. HEK293T cells were inoculated in 12-well plates and 96-well plates, respectively, and then treated with the dilution solution for 48 h. The cell viability in the 96-well plate was determined by the CCK-8 method. The experiment was repeated 8 times. Total RNA was extracted from the cells in the 12-well plates according to the instructions of the test kit (RM201, Vazyme, Nanjing, China), and the expression levels of related genes (STAT3, BCL2, MAPK3 and TNF) were detected using the RT-qPCR method (R323-01, Vazyme, Nanjing, China) with the 2−ΔΔCt method. All reaction systems and reaction temperatures were carried out in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Each group was repeated with 3 biological replicates. β-Actin was used as the reference gene. The primer sequences are shown in Supplementary Materials. 2.6. Evaluation of Candidate Compound Intervention Against Viral RdRp Proteins The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) protein sequences of Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) were retrieved from the NCBI database (accession numbers: ALI59821.1 for HTNV and UYS55322.1 for SEOV). Sequence alignment was performed using DNAMAN software (version 5.0). Three-dimensional structural models of the HTNV and SEOV RdRp proteins were subsequently generated using SWISS-MODEL (, accessed on 3 June 2026). full_text_sections.full_text: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization Simple Summary Hantaan virus, carried by rodents, causes severe bleeding and kidney disease in humans, making it a key concern for veterinary wildlife surveillance. Using computational methods, we studied early viral effects on human cells and screened for natural compounds. Three immune genes, CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10, were strongly activated early. Among six compounds, quercetin was most promising, with predicted good absorption and low toxicity. Further analysis indicated that quercetin may promote cell viability and suppress inflammation, thereby protecting cells from damage induced by HTNV infection. In baseline pharmacological assays using uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin at 3.9–7.8 μM was non-toxic, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted quercetin binds to the viral RNA polymerase at Lys884 and Arg892. These findings propose quercetin as a computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses. Abstract Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses, enveloped segmented negative-sense RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. They are predominantly maintained in rodent reservoir species, with which they have co-evolved a persistent, typically asymptomatic infection. Infected rodents do not manifest overt disease but sustain long-term viral carriage, with continuous shedding of infectious particles via excretory routes, namely urine, feces, and saliva. Human infection occurs through inhalation of virus-contaminated aerosols, direct contact with contaminated fomites or wounds, or, less frequently, via the digestive tract, leading to two severe clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS). Orthohantavirus hantaanense (Hantaan virus, HTNV) is the predominant etiological agent of HFRS in Asia, with reported case-fatality rates approaching 15%. Importantly, the occurrence of HTNV infection is not determined solely by viral or host factors. Human exposure is closely associated with the abundance, distribution, and infection status of rodent hosts, as well as the frequency of human–rodent contact. Rodent population dynamics and virus shedding are further influenced by environmental and ecological conditions, including climate variability, habitat characteristics, agricultural activities, and food availability and storage. Consequently, HTNV represents a typical One Health-related challenge in which viral maintenance in animals, environmental contamination, and human exposure are interconnected. Currently, no approved drug is available to break the aforementioned connection. Moreover, the clinical management of HTNV-infected cases still relies mainly on supportive treatment. In previous reports, ribavirin, a broad-spectrum nucleoside analog, has shown antiviral activity against hantaviruses and has been used in certain clinical settings. However, its therapeutic utility is limited by treatment timing and adverse effects, including hemolytic anemia and other treatment-related complications. Addressing these problems requires a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of HTNV and the exploration of potential drug candidates. After HTNV infection, on one hand, its own encoded proteins, such as nucleocapsid protein (NP) and glycoprotein (Gn/Gc), can inhibit the production of type I interferons by targeting the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling pathway, thereby suppressing the early warning system of the host’s innate immunity. In addition, NP can recruit and interact with fatty acid synthase (FASN), regulating lipid synthesis activity, providing necessary metabolic support for viral replication. On the other hand, HTNV infection can also activate the HIF-1 signaling pathway, aggravating barrier dysfunction and vascular leakage. Clinical studies have confirmed that the earlier the intervention is carried out for HTNV infection, the higher the cure rate for the patients. Therefore, identifying the targets of the early interaction between HTNV and the host and using these targets to explore potential candidate drugs is an effective way to address the one health-related threats posed by HTNV. By integrating omics results, compound databases, and computer-aided drug design, a systematic framework has been established to elucidate the interactions between bioactive compounds and complex biological networks. The framework integrating omics and computational drug design can not only discover antiviral drugs that protect humans, but also the host pathways it reveals may provide clues for understanding the persistence mechanism of pathogens in rodents. From the perspective of One Health, this means that intervention strategies can simultaneously address both “reducing human cases” and “understanding the maintenance mechanism of rodents”. For instance, Msobo et al. combined LC–MS-based metabolomics with network pharmacology to investigate the anti-SARS-CoV-2 potential of Salvia aurea and Salvia dolomitica, thereby identifying 83 phytochemicals predicted to interact strongly with multiple SARS-CoV-2-associated targets. Accordingly, the present study adopted a target-oriented strategy that integrates bioinformatics, network pharmacology, and molecular docking, together with preliminary in vitro transcriptomic and cytotoxicity assessments in uninfected cells, to generate hypotheses regarding natural compounds capable of modulating HTNV-related host respon…

papers.title: Predicting the potential distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Southwest China using the ecological niche modeling.
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) poses a substantial public health burden in China. With its complex topography and rich biodiversity, Southwest China has historically been an endemic area for this natural focal disease. Currently, traditional environmental factors associated with transmission here are increasingly outweighed by anthropogenic forces, notably population agglomeration. Driven by these shifting dynamics, HFRS incidence and endemic ranges are expanding, yet systematic, regional-scale assessments remain scarce. Consequently, this study employs ecological niche modeling to map potential high-risk zones. Ultimately, we aim to explore the primary factors associated with HFRS prevalence amid the complex interplay of natural environments and human activities. Methods Surveillance data of HFRS cases in Southwest China from 2014 to 2023 were obtained from the China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP). A Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model was constructed by integrating occurrence records with multisource environmental variables, including meteorological, socioeconomic, and land cover factors. Model performance was evaluated using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC), and the Jackknife test was employed to quantify the contribution of each variable. Results The MaxEnt model demonstrated robust predictive performance with a mean AUC of 0.902. Population density was identified as the predominant predictor (73.5% contribution), followed by the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) in May (9.2%) and annual mean temperature (5.8%). The spatial distribution of risk exhibited a core aggregation with sporadic dispersion pattern, with high-risk zones concentrated in the Chengdu-Chongqing urban agglomeration and localized clusters in Yunnan Province. Response curves revealed a sigmoidal positive correlation between population density and disease risk. Meteorological factors, such as temperature and precipitation, exhibited non-linear inverted U-shaped and U-shaped relationships, constraining the spatial boundaries of transmission. Conclusions The spatial heterogeneity of HFRS in Southwest China is jointly driven by anthropogenic activities and natural environmental constraints. Human population density is identified as a primary factor associated with amplified transmission risk, which may reflect the human behavior amplification effect in natural focal diseases. These findings suggest a strategic shift from blanket prevention to precision control, prioritizing active surveillance in densely populated urban fringes and areas undergoing infrastructure development.

The spatial distribution of risk exhibited a core aggregation with sporadic dispersion pattern, with high-risk zones concentrated in the Chengdu-Chongqing urban agglomeration and localized clusters in Yunnan Province. Graphical Abstract Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a natural focal disease caused by hantavirus infection, characterized primarily by acute onset, rapid disease progression, and a high mortality rate. China is one of the countries most severely affected by HFRS globally. Since the 1980s, the annual reported case count exceeded 100,000 for many years, placing a sustained and significant burden on the public health system. Although the national HFRS incidence rate in China has declined significantly in recent years following the implementation of comprehensive control measures—such as vaccination, reservoir host control, and health education—this trend does not indicate that epidemic risk has been eliminated, given the continued occurrence of sporadic cases and localized clusters. Notably, the epidemiological pattern of HFRS is not static but rather undergoes continuous evolution, driven by the interplay of natural environmental and socioeconomic factors. Particularly in the context of global warming, alterations in temperature and precipitation patterns can indirectly modulate hantavirus transmission risk by influencing the population dynamics and habitat distribution of reservoir hosts such as rodents, thereby contributing to a geographical shift in high-risk areas. Against this backdrop, the epidemiological pattern of HFRS, traditionally predominant in northern regions, is currently exhibiting new characteristics of spatial variation. In recent years, the epidemiological dynamics of HFRS in Southwest China have attracted increasing attention due to rising incidence and the region’s unique ecological landscape. While traditional high-incidence areas have long been concentrated in Northeast China and the North China Plain, Southwest China has recently exhibited an upward trend in reported cases and a gradual expansion of the endemic range, emerging as a potential high-risk region that warrants attention within the national prevention and control framework. The study area is characterized by complex topography, featuring the coexistence of plateaus, mountains, and basins, diverse climatic types, and significant ecological heterogeneity; consequently, its natural conditions differ markedly from traditional HFRS-endemic areas. This unique physiographical and climatic context may result in distinct reservoir species compositions, transmission pathways, and environmental associated factors compared to the northern endemic areas, thereby shaping a region-specific pattern of HFRS transmission. Previous studies have demonstrated that meteorological factors, socioeconomic factors, and land cover variables are closely associated with the occurrence of HFRS. However, existing literature has largely concentrated on specific HFRS-endemic cities in southwestern China, with a primary emphasis on analyzing demographic characteristics and the spatiotemporal dynamics of the epidemic. Consequently, systematic and quantitative assessments regarding the distributional characteristics of HFRS risk factors and projected risk patterns at a holistic regional scale remain insufficient. Given these limitations, it is imperative to conduct a comprehensive analysis of multidimensional influencing factors at a broader spatial scale. Therefore, this study aims to systematically identify the combined effects of meteorological, socioeconomic, and land cover variables on the occurrence of HFRS in southwestern China, delineate potential disease risk zones, and quantify the population exposed to varying levels of risk, thereby providing a scientific basis for comprehensively assessing the associated public health burden and formulating region-specific prevention and control strategies. Methods Study area Map of the study area. The figure illustrates the geographical location and elevation gradient of Southwest China Southwestern China is located between approximately 97°21′–110°11′ E and 21°08′–34°19′ N, situated at the eastern margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and encompassing the main body of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau. The region covers a total area of approximately 1.14 million km2 (Fig. 1). The region exhibits diverse climatic types, predominantly characterized by a subtropical monsoon climate alongside features of a plateau mountain climate. The mean annual temperature ranges from 8 to 20 °C, with annual precipitation typically falling between 800 and 1800 mm. Notably, significant vertical climate differentiation is observed in local alpine valley areas. According to the 2021 provincial statistical yearbooks and data from the Seventh National Population Census, the permanent resident population totaled approximately 198 million by the end of 2020. The population distribution is characterized by relative concentrations in basins, plains, and urban areas, in contrast to the sparsely populated mountainous regions. Data collection Surveillance data regarding HFRS cases in Southwest China spanning from 2014 to 2023 were sourced from the Infectious Disease Reporting System of the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC). All reported cases were confirmed strictly following the standardized diagnostic criteria formulated by the national CDC. The base map was obtained from the National Platform for Common Geospatial Information Services (https://www.tianditu.gov.cn/; Map Approval No. GS(2024)0650), featuring polygon vector layers for provincial, prefectural, and county-level administrative divisions. Population data for southwestern China were derived from the Seventh National Population Census conducted in 2020, accessed via the National Bureau of Statistics of China (https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/pcsj/rkpc/7rp/zk/indexce.htm). Population density was calculated by dividing the population size by the land area of each county. Environmental variables Definitions and types of environmental variables Variable classification Variable name Definition Resolution Variable type Climatic MAT Annual mean temperature 1 km Continuous AAP Annual average precipitation 1 km Continuous RH Average annual relative humidity 1 km Continuous Geographical LD Land cover 1 km Categorical DEM Digital elevation model 1 km Continuous Aspect Terrain aspect 1 km Continuous Slope Terrain slope 1 km Continuous NDVI3 Normalized difference vegetation index in March 1 km Continuous NDVI5 Normalized difference vegetation index in May 1 km Continuous NDVI7 Normalized difference vegetation index in July 1 km Continuous NDVI8 Normalized difference vegetation index in August 1 km Continuous NDVI9 Normalized difference vegetation index in September 1 km Continuous Socioeconomic DP Density of population 1 km Continuous To investigate the environmental risk factors influencing the spatiotemporal distribution of HFRS in recent years, we collected data on a range of environmental variables, including meteorological factors and land cover (Table 1). The selection of these variables was informed by prior studies. Meteorological data for southwestern China spanning from 2014 to 2023 were obtained from the China Meteorological Data Service Centre (https://data.cma.cn/). The meteorological variables included in this study comprised the multi-year mean relative humidity, multi-year mean temperature, and multi-year mean precipitation. Using ArcGIS 10.8 software (ESRI, Redlands, CA, USA), raster layers representing the mean meteorological data for the 2014–2023 period were generated via the Kriging interpolation method. Elevation data were derived from a nationwide Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km, obtained from the National Earth System Science Data Center (http://www.geodata.cn/data/datadetails.html?dataguid=201519481253546&docid=1301). Additionally, slope and aspect variables were calculated from the elevation data using ArcGIS 10.8 software. Land use data for the year 2013 were obtained from the National Earth System Science Data Center (https://www.geodata.cn/), provided as a raster layer with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km. Although these data slightly precede the case collection period (2014–2023), they maintain strong representativeness, as the macro-scale land cover patterns and regional ecological landscapes in Southwest China remained relatively stable over this decade, thereby serving as a reliable baseline without diminishing the model’s explanatory power. Data for the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were obtained from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (https://www.tpdc.ac.cn/). As the most widely used vegetation index, NDVI indicates vegetation growth status and coverage, thereby comprehensively reflecting the environmental conditions of the region. All environmental variable datasets were projected to a unified geographic coordinate system and converted into raster format. Subsequently, the data were resampled to a consistent spatial resolution of 1 km and clipped to the extent of the study area using vector boundary data in ArcGIS 10.8. Statistical methods Prior to model construction, to ensure the robustness and interpretability of the analytical results, we constructed an initial set of variables by systematically reviewing existing literature to screen for potential environmental factors associated with the occurrence of HFRS. All candidate variables were entered into the MaxEnt model for a preliminary run, with the number of replicates set to 1. The Jackknife test was subsequently employed to evaluate the contribution and importance of each variable to the model. To prevent model overfitting and potential interference with result interpretation caused by the coexistence of highly correlated variables, we subsequently conducted a multicollinearity test using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis, establishing a threshold of 0.8 (|r|≥ 0.8). For pairs of highly correlated variables, selection was prioritized based on contribution metrics derived from the preliminary model run: the variable with the higher contribution was retained, while the lower-contributing variable was excluded. Ultimately, a final set of variables that were mutually independent and possessed significant explanatory power for HFRS transmission risk was selected to construct the final model. Ecological niche modeling Model construction In this study, the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt, version 3.4.3) model was employed for ecological niche modeling. Based on the principle of maximum entropy, this model predicts the probability of presence in specific habitats by integrating geographic occurrence records of HFRS cases with environmental background points; it is widely recognized as a robust machine learning method characterized by high predictive accuracy. Model training and parameter optimization To construct a high-precision predictive model, the key eco-environmental factors identified during the screening process were incorporated into the MaxEnt model. In terms of data partitioning, 75% of the HFRS occurrence records were randomly selected as the training set for model calibration, while the remaining 25% were reserved as the test set for model validation. To minimize random errors associated with single simulations and enhance the stability of the results, the model was executed with 10 replicates, and the final output was derived from the average of these 10 runs. Apart from these specific settings, all other parameters were maintained at the software’s default values. Default settings were retained because previous studies have demonstrated their robustness in ecological niche modeling when sufficient occurrence records are available. Model performance evaluation The predictive performance of the model was evaluated primarily using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). The AUC values range from 0 to 1, with a value closer to 1 indicating superior predictive performance. Specifically, an AUC of 0.5 represents a random prediction. The performance levels are categorized as follows: 0.5–0.6 is considered poor; 0.7–0.8 is fair; 0.8–0.9 is good; and 0.9–1.0 is excellent. Furthermore, a threshold-dependent binomial test was employed, utilizing the omission rate as a test statistic to comprehensively evaluate the statistical significance of the model and assess the potential for overfitting. Analysis of environmental variable importance To identify the key driving factors influencing the distribution of HFRS, the Jackknife test was employed to quantitatively evaluate the contribution of each environmental variable to the model gain, thereby identifying the dominant variables containing the most critical information. Additionally, response curves were utilized to analyze the non-linear response patterns of the predicted probability of HFRS occurrence to variations in individual variables, thereby elucidating the quantitative relationships between environmental factors and disease risk. Risk zonation and population exposure assessment The output of the MaxEnt model consists of continuous probability values ranging from 0 to 1, representing the environmental suitability for the occurrence of HFRS (i.e., the potential risk). The continuous suitability values predicted by MaxEnt were reclassified into three risk levels (low, medium, and high risk) following the classification scheme proposed by Acharya et al., where suitability values ≤0.29, 0.29–0.45, and >0.45 represent low-, medium-, and high-risk areas, respectively. This approach has been previously applied in ecological niche modeling studies and facilitates interpretation of spatial risk patterns. Finally, a spatial overlay analysis was performed using ArcGIS software to integrate the reclassified risk zonation map with population raster data. This process allowed for the quantitative estimation of the size and spatial distribution characteristics of the population exposed to varying risk levels at both the prefectural and regional scales. Results Descriptive analysis results The mean annual incidence rate in Southwestern China was 0.19 per 100,000 population, with the rate reaching 0.32 per 100,000 in 2023. Furthermore, HFRS cases exhibited pronounced seasonal fluctuations, characterized by a primary peak during the spring–summer period (April–June) and a secondary peak during the autumn–winter period (November–January). In terms of geographic distribution, the Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan Province, along with the Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture and Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Yunnan Province, were identified as the primary high-incidence areas. Collectively, these three regions accounted for 62.60% of the total cases reported in Southwestern China. Demographic analysis indicated that males and farmers aged 20–60 years constituted the primary high-risk groups. The incidence rate among males was 45.01 per 100,000 population, significantly exceeding that among females (1.76 per 100,000 population).
